MOVING TARGETS

By: Nicky Troll | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
There is a new level to the fight against crime. Powerful suspects are fighting back – not just silencing the whistleblowers, but now it seems they’ve set their sights on the investigators threate

Unique Selling Point:
A bigger picture look at worrying crime trend without the speculation, but with the grit.

Summary:
In the first two weeks of July there was an assassination in JHB and an attempted hit in DBN. The targets – people investigating high level crime and corruption.

Professional South Africans walking the line in an attempt to see justice served to those behind grosse fraud and corruption are now at the frontlines – increasingly become targets.

In this piece we explore the shift, the shortfalls and what needs to happen to ensure success in the fight against crime while questioning what needs to happen to protect those at the frontlines.

Further information:
The effects of targeted killings go far beyond the pulling of a trigger: they threaten a country’s security, politics, judiciary and economy, and create an atmosphere of fear and intimidation that warps the fabric of society.

Since 2012, there has been a 62% increase in the murder rate. In that time, the ability of the SAPS to solve murders has more than halved, dropping by 55% so that in the past 2021/22 financial year, only 14.5% of murder cases were closed.
South Africa has witnessed the crippling of its police, including its critical crime intelligence function, through years of mismanagement, capacity shortages, political interference, deep-seated corruption, haemorrhaging of specialist skills and a failure to conduct intelligence-based investigations.
The police have been unable to take meaningful steps to address the underlying drivers of increasing violence, including targeted killings, in South Africa: the proliferation of illegal firearms, pools of hitmen being spawned in the largely unregulated taxi industry, and organised criminal gangs in the Western Cape.
Also to be noted, we have VIP protection units – paid for by taxpayers to protect ministers, when they should be protecting the frontline in the fight against crime. If government can’t protect these people – what chance does justice stand?
THE SIU head Andy Mothibi said in an article earlier this year that the modern criminal had become adept at corrupting state officials and functionaries – and, when his graft-busting squad descended, they faced an onslaught of attacks and death threats.
“When they realise that we are uncovering what they have done, things become dangerous and often lethal,” Mothibi said, adding that white collar crime had become intertwined with organised syndicates who did not hesitate in targeting whistle-blowers and investigators.

INTERVIEWS

 CORRUPTION WATCH - A GROUP THAT WILL SPEAK TO THE THREAT ON DEMOCRACY // RISK TO CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM
 GITOC – RUMBI MATAMBA – THE BUSINESS OF KILLING – SHE WILL SPEAK TO MO’s AND DANGERS OF A SPIRALLING CRIME TREND NOW FOCUSSED ON THE NEXT LEVEL OF CRIME FIGHTERS
 FORMER MAJOR GENERAL JOHAN BOOYSEN – THE PITFALLS OF LAW ENFORCEMENT – CHASING DOWN MINIONS INSTEAD OF MASTERMINDS
o ALTERNATIVE: GARETH NEWHAM – ISS – extensive research on police inefficiencies
 UNDERWORLD ELEMENT TO ECHO THE EXPERTS / MO’s


TREATMENT
I’m thinking like an espionage / tense feel…. so moody lighting, slider on second cam. And then some stylized shots around documents, money and sneaky calls… We’ll use archive of hits caught on camera. Will speak to Jan about some kind of graphic treatment for the images of the targeted professionals











Extra Budget Items:
1. Trip to CPT. Booysen and Karam Singh is in CPT.
2. We’ll need to get some images of assassinated or targeted persons.

STRUCTURE – MOVING TARGETS

VO: It's not a new trend. Not globally. And certainly not in South Africa.

Here, there are at least three assassinations every week.

VISUAL MOMENT WITH HITS CCTV FOOTAGE

VO: But, the targets are shifting…

LINK: // as the fight against corruption intensifies, the fight back from powerful suspects is too. If they can’t make the case go away, they’ll make the person investigating them go away.

VO : In this story, we examine how criminals are setting their sights on the people trying to bring them to book… with insights from a former top cop…..

BOOYSEN: // it's an attack on, the rule of law.

VO: A crime analyst…..

THOBELA: It is very hard to // link // the mastermind and the minion,

VO: An anti-corruption champion…

KARAM: // there is this violent response to the fight against corruption //.

VO: And….a man in the killing business.

VISUALS WALKING IN, UP THE STAIRS **

VO: Everything about this interview is secretive, he’ll wear a mask throughout our interaction, determined not to reveal his identity. A conversation as unsettling as it is deeply uncomfortable

C – how does it make you feel - you get paid to kill people?
H - What ever someone says, I don’t care. I’m just waiting for that opportunity to go and work and get money – that is it.

VO: 11 July 2024 - Zenzele Benedict Sithole, a veteran corruption investigator in the City of Joburg, is navigating afternoon traffic. At an intersection a gunman approaches on foot and opens fire, fatally wounding him.

18 July 2024 – then just seven days later in a Durban hotel parking lot, two gunmen approach Coreth [KOE-RETH] Naude while she's in her car. They open fire, hitting her in the upper body, neck and face. Naude, who survives the shooting, is an advocate working for SARS, investigating several high profile tax related cases.

Both in broad daylight, both targets, investigating high-level crime and corruption..

They’ll likely not be the last investigators targeted for assassination… and they weren’t the first.

▪ Lt Col FRANS MATHIPA from the HAWKS – investigating alleged abductions by the SANDF. 6 August 2023
▪ LT Col CHARL KINNEAR – Western Cape Anti-gang unit detective… probing some of the country’s worst violent offenders. 18 September 2020
▪ CLOETE MURRAY, a prominent liquidator and his son, Tom, a legal advisor handling tricky high-profile cases. 18 March 2023
▪ BABITA DEOKARAN – A Gauteng Health Department Finance Manager who blew the whistle on corruption. 23 August 2021

All of them dead now.

INTRO KARAM: My name is Karam Singh. I'm the executive director at Corruption Watch.

KARAM: // These are not people that are necessarily sticking their necks out. They’re people that are just doing their jobs. They're doing their jobs without fear, favor, or prejudice. But the environment now is placing them under threat.

VO: In most assassinations, not much is ever known about the motive and who provided the cash. But the methods used, the business of killing, is often similar.

And what drives the gunmen is always the same.

INTRO BOOYSEN: I'm Johan Booysen, former major general, South African Police head of the HAWKS, KwaZulu-Natal.

BOOYSEN: If you look at the pool of, //assassins, they do them with it's a political killing or a taxi killing or, each on a, love triangle, issue. They they don't care to them as long as they get their money. The higher the stakes, the more money will be available to to pay for the assassin. So it varies if if it's high stakes and if it's high profile.

H – For money, sister, I’ll do anything for money there’s no way I can say no, we don’t think about risk, the only thing we think about is money.

INTRO THOBELA: I am Chwayita THOBELA: and I am a research analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, and I work on the Assassin Asian Monitor, and we look at targeted killings in South Africa.

THOBELA: We have seen, organized crime hit. That was it was alleged that it cost a million rand. We have also then on the other spectrum, seen personal hits going for as little as 3.5 thousand rand. so the price varies. // with the right amount of money, you can get a hit against someone.

VO: The most this killer has been paid for a single hit was R150 000 for a politically connected target.. High-profile hits usually come with a deadline.

H – // they give you a specific time before this date you have to do this job. // you have to make sure by this day you have to be done.
C – explain to me step by step who to kill
H – they give me a photo of the person I have to kill, and they give me the location of where he stays, and so I have to go there and check my job how I am going to get that person, what time he wakes up , what time he comes in and where he goes, and what he’s doing during the day. I have to decide how and when to kill this person.

VO: These hits aren’t opportunistic, they’re meticulously planned .

LINK: // The victims often would have had eyes on them for days, if not weeks or months. Unaware that they’ve been tailed, that they’re routines have been plotted.

VO: Sometimes there’s inside information from people close to the target.

H – There is somebody that is informing us that there is a person that will be at, let me say, at Pretoria at this time. That’s why when that person leaves we have to follow him with a car. // The way I am working, I have to trace him until I get him and then I finish him.
H - Sometimes we kill them when they’re on their way, sometimes in their houses,//you have to stay ready always, when you see that chance, you have to use it.

KARAM: // What we see increasingly with the kind of brazen criminal activity is a lack of respect for the rule of law and ultimately a culture in the country where when you get in trouble with the law, you seek extra judicial means to get around it, as opposed to, facing your accusers and facing your charges.

VO: So, with the law closing in on powerful suspects, they’re becoming increasingly desperate to cover their tracks. And whistleblowers and witnesses are no longer the only ones at risk.

These assassinations are a sign of the fightback from organized criminals against those uncovering their fraud and corruption.

BOOYSEN: // you need to look at to the people all that are being investigated. The majority of those people are high profile people. // People in places of power. The more the, the noose tightens, the more panicky they will get // I think in their mind it's probably the only way out for them other than facing orange overalls.

THOBELA: if you are to do your job and you continue doing this, then there is a possibility that you'll be a victim of violence. // // it's sending a very chilling message, not only to those who are involved in the investigation, but to everyone in that sector

VO : As a consequence, justice is further delayed in an environment where investigators already struggle to keep up with the caseload. And, as things stand, even the investigations into the assassinations are falling short.

THOBELA: There's a motive behind taking someone out right. And the hitman is only a third party who is brought in to take out this person. And in most cases the hitman will be arrested but not the mastermind.

BOOYSEN: / There's been a couple of cases recently where it's evident who could have been behind the assassination. // after they've arrested the footsoldiers, they seem to stop it because then they feel that they've solved the crime. They've not solved the crime

VO: The paymasters are ultimately protected through a network of middlemen.

BOOYSEN: That's normally very rare that the person who does the actual assassination has direct links with the person behind it. They will use intermediaries. And I think that's what makes it more challenging for investigators to get to the bottom of who is actually behind it.

VO: It’s about referrals, connections and trust.

H –//there’s no way that someone can come to you they have to send somebody
H –// One person connects you to another person and they connect you to another person.
C – Would you ever give up the middleman.
H – If they catch me, I will stand for everything, I won’t say anything about who sent me. //
C – is there more than one middle man in a high profile case
H – Sometimes it is like that, sister. You will never know, they just give you the job for you to.

VO: While the murder rate has climbed in the last decade. Just under 15% of murder cases are actually solved in South Africa.

BOOYSEN: //these cases are being investigated on a, on a transactional basis. They investigate the actual killing, and that's where it stops. They don't go beyond that. they should focus the investigation on the motive, look at what's behind it, no matter how long it takes. //

VO: So, as this complex and sinister crime trend takes route, what can be done?

KARAM: we need an enhanced whistleblower protection system. We need a dedicated anti-corruption agency. But none of these items alone is going to resolve the issue. we do spend a lot of money, providing VIP security to, prominent persons to, politicians, to members of cabinet. So, I mean, if we're thinking about risk profiling, who's really under threat? is it, is it cabinet ministers or is it these frontline forensic workers?

VO: For as long as the masterminds aren’t being caught, the business of killing has the potential to spiral out of control.

LINK: But when one trigger puller is arrested, another is ready to take his place. Ironically Hitmen are as disposable as their targets.

H – This is a way of making money quick-quick. You go for three days, five days, 15 days, you come back with R250 000. Who can give you that money?

VO: The impacts of targeted killings extend beyond jeopardizing the rule of law and our country’s security. They foster an atmosphere of fear and intimidation where, no sooner have they begun, investigations hit a dead end.

 
PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: The paymasters behind targeted killings evade prosecution through a network of middlemen.

BOOYSEN: That's normally very rare that the person who does the actual assassination has direct links with the person behind it.

VO: We interrogate the inner workings of the killing business..

PROMO 2
VO: In a shocking new trend, Witnesses and Whistleblowers are no longer the only ones being targeted in the fight back from organised crime.

Powerful suspects are setting their sights on those out to bring them to book.

THOBELA: if you are to do your job and you continue doing this, then there is a possibility that you'll be a victim of violence.

PROMO 3
VO: Assassinations targeting professionals fighting organised crime are on the rise, with powerful suspects seemingly looking to ruthless hitmen, to make high profile cases go away.

H – //I’ll do anything for money // we don’t think about risk, the only thing we think about is money.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: A bigger picture look at worrying crime trend without the speculation, but with the grit.
metadata.Summary: In the first two weeks of July there was an assassination in JHB and an attempted hit in DBN. The targets – people investigating high level crime and corruption. Professional South Africans walking the line in an attempt to see justice served to those behind grosse fraud and corruption are now at the frontlines – increasingly become targets. In this piece we explore the shift, the shortfalls and what needs to happen to ensure success in the fight against crime while questioning what needs to happen to protect those at the frontlines.
metadata.Further information: The effects of targeted killings go far beyond the pulling of a trigger: they threaten a country’s security, politics, judiciary and economy, and create an atmosphere of fear and intimidation that warps the fabric of society. Since 2012, there has been a 62% increase in the murder rate. In that time, the ability of the SAPS to solve murders has more than halved, dropping by 55% so that in the past 2021/22 financial year, only 14.5% of murder cases were closed. South Africa has witnessed the crippling of its police, including its critical crime intelligence function, through years of mismanagement, capacity shortages, political interference, deep-seated corruption, haemorrhaging of specialist skills and a failure to conduct intelligence-based investigations. The police have been unable to take meaningful steps to address the underlying drivers of increasing violence, including targeted killings, in South Africa: the proliferation of illegal firearms, pools of hitmen being spawned in the largely unregulated taxi industry, and organised criminal gangs in the Western Cape. Also to be noted, we have VIP protection units – paid for by taxpayers to protect ministers, when they should be protecting the frontline in the fight against crime. If government can’t protect these people – what chance does justice stand? THE SIU head Andy Mothibi said in an article earlier this year that the modern criminal had become adept at corrupting state officials and functionaries – and, when his graft-busting squad descended, they faced an onslaught of attacks and death threats. “When they realise that we are uncovering what they have done, things become dangerous and often lethal,” Mothibi said, adding that white collar crime had become intertwined with organised syndicates who did not hesitate in targeting whistle-blowers and investigators.
